subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (x, a, a), (a, x, a) and (a, a, x) is equal to (x + 2a)(x − a)².

mark_split.label: Take out the common factor x + 2a
Apply R₂ → R₂ − R₁ and R₃ → R₃ − R₁

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.45, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 16. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape gives one mark to each of the four independent moves — the column addition that produces the equal entries, the factoring, the two row subtractions that make the determinant triangular, and the diagonal product — because each can be right or wrong on its own and a student who reaches the triangular form has clearly earned three of four. Independently checked before authoring, by two numerical substitutions: x = 5, a = 2 gives determinant 81 and (5+4)(3)² = 81; x = 1, a = −3 gives determinant −80 and (1−6)(4)² = −80. Both sides agree. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices supplies one of them. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say which column operation you start with, what comes out as a factor, which rows you subtract, and how you finish.

steps.label: Add the columns
steps.margin_note: First mark. Every row of this determinant adds up to the same thing, x + 2a. Adding all three columns into the first is what makes that visible.
steps.memory_tip: Every row here adds up to x + 2a, so add all three columns into the first.

lines.text: \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} x & a & a \\ a & x & a \\ a & a & x \end{vmatrix}

lines: Every row adds up to x + 2a, so apply

lines.text: \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} x+2a & a & a \\ x+2a & x & a \\ x+2a & a & x \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That all three columns are added into the first, because every row of this determinant has the same total x + 2a.
accept: add column two and column three to column one because every row sums to x plus two a
apply C one goes to C one plus C two plus C three
each row adds up to the same value so put that in the first column
prathi row sum x plus two a, so columns anni C one lo kalapali
the column operation makes the first column constant
heard_as: C one plus C two plus C three

steps.why: The determinant is symmetric in the sense that every row has the same total. Adding the columns is the standard way to turn that hidden fact into a visible common factor.
common_mistakes: Adding the ROWS instead of the columns, which does not give a constant column.
Writing x + 2a as x + a because only one a was added.

steps.label: Take out x + 2a
steps.margin_note: Second mark. A factor common to every entry of one COLUMN comes out of the determinant once. Column 1 becomes all 1s.
steps.memory_tip: A factor common to a whole column comes out once, and leaves that column as all 1s.
lines: Column 1 now has x + 2a in every position,
so take it out of the determinant.

lines.text: \Delta = (x+2a)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a \\ 1 & x & a \\ 1 & a & x \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That x + 2a is common to the whole first column and comes out of the determinant once, leaving 1s in that column.
accept: take x plus two a out of the first column leaving ones
the common factor comes outside the determinant once
factor x plus two a out of column one
first column nunchi x plus two a bayataki teeyali
pull the common bracket in front and the column becomes all ones

steps.why: This is the first of the two brackets in the answer, and it is now fixed. Everything that follows only has to produce (x − a)².
common_mistakes: Taking the factor out three times, once for each entry of the column.
Leaving 0 instead of 1 in the first column after removing the factor.

steps.label: Subtract R₁
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Subtracting row 1 from rows 2 and 3 clears the first column below the top and leaves x − a in one position of each row. The determinant is now triangular.
steps.memory_tip: Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3 — the zeros below the diagonal make it triangular.
lines: Apply R₂ → R₂ − R₁ and R₃ → R₃ − R₁.
R₂ becomes (0, x − a, 0) and R₃ becomes

recall.must_convey: That row 1 is subtracted from rows 2 and 3, giving zeros in the first column and x − a in the remaining positions, so the determinant becomes triangular.
accept: subtract row one from row two and from row three
R two minus R one and R three minus R one give zeros below the diagonal
the row operations leave x minus a on the diagonal and zeros under it
row one ni row two, row three nunchi teeste triangular form vasthundi
after subtracting row one the determinant is upper triangular

steps.why: The SAME row 1 is subtracted from both row 2 and row 3, not one of those rows from the other. That is what leaves a zero in every position of those rows except one, which is what makes the final step a single multiplication.
common_mistakes: Using R₃ → R₃ − R₂ instead of R₃ − R₁, which leaves no triangular form.
Writing a − x instead of x − a and flipping the sign twice over.

steps.label: Multiply the diagonal
steps.margin_note: Last mark. For a triangular determinant the value is just the product of the diagonal entries: 1 × (x − a) × (x − a).
steps.memory_tip: A triangular determinant is just the product of its diagonal entries.

equals the product of its diagonal entries:

recall.must_convey: That a triangular determinant equals the product of its diagonal entries, giving (x − a)², which with the factor already taken out gives the required result.
accept: a triangular determinant is the product of the diagonal so we get x minus a squared
one times x minus a times x minus a gives x minus a whole squared

triangular determinant ki diagonal product ne answer
the diagonal gives x minus a squared so the result follows

steps.why: Expanding a triangular determinant along the first column gives one term, and the same happens again inside it. Naming the diagonal rule saves both expansions.
common_mistakes: Expanding the full 3×3 by cofactors and making an arithmetic slip.
Writing (x − a) once instead of squared.
